newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Tory leader pacifies separatists.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Tory leader pacifies separatists.

text.p: If Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien wins the Canadian election on June 2, Montmagny resident Alain Robin says he wants Quebec to split from Canada.
But if federalist Tory leader Jean Charest wins, Robin says he will be quite happy to support him in keeping Canada together.

"Jean Chretien, I believe, does not help Quebec," Robin said this weekend as he carried his groceries in this town south of Quebec City. "Canada should stay together, but under Jean Charest, not under Chretien."
Robin, 45, like many voters in Quebec, has been seduced by Charest's upbeat and emotional message of reconciliation with Canada.

Charest has spent an intense two days crossing Quebec to capitalise on his personal popularity and his recent surge in pre-election polls. He said Saturday he hoped to win at least 40 of Quebec's 75 seats, a significant leap from the Conservative party's current one Quebec seat -- Charest's.
His main message throughout the campaign has been to convince Canadians he can resolve the schism between French-speaking Quebec and the rest of the country.

"I'm asking you to help me, because the message that you send today is a message that will echo elsewhere in Canada," Charest urged an emotional crowd of supporters as he passed through Montmagny. "It's important that elsewhere in Canada they know that Quebeckers are now ready to work on a common project, that they share the same values and they want the country to work."
His unity speech roused an impromptu signing of the national anthem in Riviere-du-Loup on the weekend, previously a separatist haven.

Quebec came perilously close to separating from Canada in a 1995 referendum. The vote against Quebec sovereignty won by less than one percent, despite Chretien's assurances that the separatist sentiment was weak.

Charest blamed Chretien, also a Quebecker, for the political uncertainty that has plagued Canada for the past two years and accuses him and the separatist Bloc Quebecois for creating "a climate of confrontation."
"It's time to reach out," 38-year-old Charest said repeatedly as he passed through Quebec. "It's time to make sure this country works."
Charest's approach is winning him widespread support in Quebec, where he has been rising quickly in the polls to the detriment of the Liberals and the Bloc Quebecois.

"I'll vote for him because of his programme. He's got a solid programme for national unity that Chretien doesn't have," said voter Martial Lemay as Charest prepared to speak in Plessisville, between Quebec City and Montreal.
"Canada has been destabilised," he said. "(Bloc Quebecois Leader Gilles) Duceppe is always looking for reasons for it not to work, but Charest has a plan."

Charest has said he would like to give the provinces more power and build so-called covenants with the provinces to deal with health care, education and inter-provincial trade. He also proposes tax cuts for individuals and businesses as a way to create jobs.
In Quebec, he is helped by the lack of personal popularity of Jean Chretien -- "the curse of Quebec" as one Quebecker said this weekend -- and by the stumbling campaign of the Bloc Quebecois.

Much of Quebec was swept by the Bloc Quebecois in the 1993 election, giving the separatist party 54 seats in the House of Commons and making the party the official opposition, despite its aims to divide Canada into pieces.
The June 2 election will likely be a close three-way race in many parts of Quebec.

But outside the province, Charest's support is dwarfed by a Liberal stronghold in Ontario, Canada's most populous province, and by widespread support in Western Canada for the right-wing Reform party. In national polls, the Tories are far behind the leading Liberals.
Chretien aims to spend the last week of the campaign fighting the Reform party in the West and the Conservatives in Quebec and the east.
